pages.name: Length of 6 − j8
pages.task: How long is the arrow `6 − j8`?
pages.why: The arrow goes 6 across and 8 down, so the triangle's short sides are 6 and 8 long. Pythagoras gives `√(36 + 64) = √100 = 10`. The length is never negative, whichever way the arrow points.

pages.name: The angle
pages.text: The angle θ is measured from the positive real axis round to the arrow, anticlockwise counting as positive. It is called the argument. In the triangle the up side, 4, is opposite θ, and the across side, 3, is next to it.

pages.name: Angle of 4 + j3
pages.task: What angle does `4 + j3` make with the positive real axis?
pages.why: The up side, 3, is opposite θ, and the across side, 4, is next to it. So `tan θ = 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75`, and `θ = tan⁻¹(0.75) = 36.87°`. The arrow points into the top right, where the calculator's answer is the right one.

pages.name: Half a turn out
pages.text: Now take `−3 − j4`, the same arrow turned half round. Its `b ÷ a` is `−4 ÷ −3`, which is `4 ÷ 3` again, so the calculator says 53.13° again. The ghost points up and right, exactly the wrong way.

pages.name: Angle of −1 − j1
pages.task: What is the angle of `−1 − j1`?
pages.why: `b ÷ a = −1 ÷ −1 = 1`, and the calculator says `tan⁻¹(1) = 45°`, pointing top right. The arrow points down and left, so take 180° away, `45° − 180° = −135°`. Its length is `√(1 + 1) = √2 = 1.414`, so `−1 − j1 = 1.414∠−135°`.

pages.name: A whole turn
pages.text: A whole turn, 360°, brings an arrow back to where it started. So adding or taking away 360° names the same arrow.

pages.name: 5∠270° in range
pages.task: Write `5∠270°` with its angle in the usual range, more than −180° and up to 180°.
pages.why: 270° is three quarter turns anticlockwise, which ends pointing straight down. Taking away a whole turn leaves it pointing the same way, `270° − 360° = −90°`. So `5∠270° = 5∠−90°`, which is `−j5`.

pages.name: Going back
pages.text: Going back is easier. The across part is the arrow's shadow on the real axis, and the up part is its shadow on the j axis. So `a = r cos θ` and `b = r sin θ`.

pages.alt: The complex plane, real across and j up. Its shadow on the real axis is 8.66 and its shadow on the j axis is 5. Its shadow on the real axis is minus 8.66. An arc marks the angle 30 degrees from the positive real axis. An arrow from 0 to 10 at an angle of 30 degrees. An arrow from 0 to 10 at an angle of 150 degrees. a equals 10 cos 30 degrees equals 10 times 0.866: 8.66. b equals 10 sin 30 degrees equals 10 times 0.5: 5. a equals 10 cos 150 degrees equals 10 times ( minus 0.866): minus 8.66. Its two names: minus 8.66 plus j5, and 10 at an angle of 150 degrees.

pages.name: 4∠120° as parts
pages.why: The across part is `4 cos 120° = 4 × (−0.5) = −2`, and the up part is `4 sin 120° = 3.464`. So `4∠120° = −2 + j3.464`. The minus comes out by itself, because the arrow's shadow on the real axis points left.

pages.name: On the axes
pages.text: An arrow along an axis needs no tan⁻¹ at all. Read its angle straight off the sketch: 0° right, 90° up, 180° left and −90° down.

pages.name: −2 + j1 in polar form
pages.task: Write `−2 + j1` in polar form, r∠θ.
pages.why: The length is `√(2² + 1²) = √5 = 2.236`. The calculator says `tan⁻¹(1 ÷ −2) = −26.57°`, which points down and right. The arrow points up and left, so add 180°, `−26.57° + 180° = 153.43°`. So `−2 + j1 = 2.236∠153.43°`.

pages.name: 10∠−36.87° as parts
pages.why: The across part is `10 cos(−36.87°) = 10 × 0.8 = 8`, and the up part is `10 sin(−36.87°) = 10 × (−0.6) = −6`. So `10∠−36.87°` is `8 − j6`. The angle is below the real axis, so the up part comes out negative by itself.
